questions.question:
Visvesvaraya Iron and Steel Plant [VISL] was started as the Mysore Iron Works on 18 January 1923 by Nalvadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar and his Diwan Sir M Visvesvaraya. It is now an integrated steel plant under the jurisdiction of the Steel Authority of India Limited.

questions.solution: (b) Public Sector Industry. It is now run by SAIL, a Government of India undertaking, so it is in the public sector.

questions.topic: Alluvial chars of the delta (printed: Soil Resources)
questions.question:
Every year, the Ganges and the Brahmaputra bring millions of tons of silt into the plains of Bangladesh. They carve new courses every year. As a result, islands are created which last until they are washed away by fresh floods. These islands are locally known as chars.
Which of the following is the primary benefit provided by the chars for the local community?

options.c: the protection from man-eating tigers of nearby Sundarbans.
options.d: deposition of mineral resources from the Himalayas, such as precious stones.

questions.solution: (b) fertile soil for subsistence farming. Chars are made of freshly deposited silt (new alluvium/khadar), which is very fertile.

questions.topic: Beyond syllabus: river rafting on torrential Himalayan rivers (printed: Health Education)
questions.question:
River Rafting is journeying on a torrential river on an inflatable rubber boat. Rivers originating at high altitudes have torrential flow near their source.
Which of the following places would be suitable for river rafting?
questions.solution: (c) Ganga in Rishikesh. Rishikesh lies where the Ganga leaves the Himalayas, close to its high-altitude source, so it flows fast and turbulent; the others are slow plains/delta rivers.

questions.topic: Traditional water harvesting - zings of Ladakh (printed: Water Resources)
questions.question:
In certain parts of India, glaciers are the main source of water. The people in these areas use an innovative water harvesting technique by diverting glacier streams into small tanks. It is usually done in the evening when the glaciers are relatively melted.
Which of these regions could be practising this?
questions.solution: (b) Ladakh region. In cold-desert Ladakh, glacial meltwater is channelled into tanks called zings; the other regions get abundant rain or are not glacier-fed.

questions.topic: Irrigation methods in the Northern Plains
concepts: Irrigation methods in the Northern Plains
questions.question:
India has had a history of famines because of rainfed agriculture and rapid population growth. After the era of the Green Revolution that began in the 1960s, India never experienced a famine-like situation; it did, however, experience a drought of the century in 1987. Northern states (Punjab, Haryana and western UP) with a high level of irrigation are contributing almost all of wheat and two-thirds of rice to the central pool of India.
(a) Mention any two methods of irrigation commonly practised in the Northern Plains of India.
questions.solution: Canal irrigation and well/tube-well irrigation.

questions.topic: Irrigation methods in the Northern Plains - reasons
concepts: Irrigation methods in the Northern Plains - reasons
questions.question:
India has had a history of famines because of rainfed agriculture and rapid population growth. After the era of the Green Revolution that began in the 1960s, India never experienced a famine-like situation; it did, however, experience a drought of the century in 1987. Northern states (Punjab, Haryana and western UP) with a high level of irrigation are contributing almost all of wheat and two-thirds of rice to the central pool of India.
(b) For each method mentioned, state why it is popular here.
questions.solution: Canals: the plains are drained by perennial, snow-fed rivers (Ganga, Yamuna, Sutlej) and the land is level, so canals can be dug easily. Wells/tube wells: the soft alluvial soil holds plenty of groundwater at shallow depth and is easy to bore, and cheap electricity runs pumps.

marking_points.point: Canals - perennial rivers and level plains
Wells/tube wells - plentiful groundwater, soft alluvium easy to dig

questions.question:
"A small sugarcane farmer in western Uttar Pradesh, Shri Raghuvir Singh, is getting on with age and is thinking of selling his land and moving out of farming. He has two sons, both graduates and working in Gurgaon. He did not make his sons farmers because farming is hard work and is non-profitable. This is the story of most farmers in India. Wealth and security of the country comes from its land, and hence, what is needed is sustainable and high productivity agriculture."
(a) High productivity in agriculture will help boost our country's industrial sector. Explain.
questions.solution: Agriculture supplies raw materials to agro-based industries (e.g. sugarcane to sugar mills, cotton to textiles, jute to jute mills); higher farm output means more and cheaper raw material, and richer farmers also create demand for industrial goods such as fertilisers, tractors and pumps.

marking_points.point: Agriculture provides raw materials to agro-based industries (with example)

questions.question:
"A small sugarcane farmer in western Uttar Pradesh, Shri Raghuvir Singh, is getting on with age and is thinking of selling his land and moving out of farming. He has two sons, both graduates and working in Gurgaon. He did not make his sons farmers because farming is hard work and is non-profitable. This is the story of most farmers in India. Wealth and security of the country comes from its land, and hence, what is needed is sustainable and high productivity agriculture."
(b) Enumerate two major problems encountered by a majority of India's farming community.
questions.solution: Any two: small and fragmented land holdings; dependence on the monsoon/insufficient irrigation; soil erosion and loss of fertility; poor-quality seeds and low use of modern inputs; low prices/indebtedness.

questions.topic: Heat waves in the Gangetic plains
concepts: Heat waves in the Gangetic plains
questions.question:
"Heatwave days highest in April in 15 years in Gangetic West Bengal." (Source: IMD)
Mention two probable reasons for the above statement.
questions.solution: (1) El Nino conditions led to an earlier and hotter onset of summer and fewer pre-monsoon thunderstorms (Kalbaisakhi/Nor'westers) that normally cool the region in April. (2) Global warming has raised average temperatures, increasing the frequency and severity of heat waves (aided by hot, dry winds and clear skies).

marking_points.point: El Nino / absence of pre-monsoon showers

questions.question:
Although landfills are the cheapest waste management strategy, they are often touted as harmful to the environment.
Name any three ways by which landfills cause harm to our environment.
questions.solution: Any three: (1) decomposing waste releases landfill gases such as methane, a greenhouse gas contributing to global warming (and a fire risk); (2) toxic leachate seeps into the ground, contaminating soil and groundwater; (3) foul odour pollutes the surroundings; (4) landfills become breeding grounds for flies, mosquitoes, rats and bacteria that spread disease; (5) they occupy large areas of land.

questions.question:
In many parts of the world, man has disturbed the ecological balance. The factors responsible are deprivation of natural habitat and discriminate killing and hunting of animals. Many birds and animals face the danger of extinction today. Many programs like social forestry and Van Mahotsava should be popularised at regional and community levels. This will increase awareness.
(a) State the human activities responsible for the loss of forest.
questions.solution: Deforestation - cutting of forests to clear land for agriculture and settlements, for timber and fuelwood, mining, construction of dams/roads/industries, and overgrazing.

questions.question:
In many parts of the world, man has disturbed the ecological balance. The factors responsible are deprivation of natural habitat and discriminate killing and hunting of animals. Many birds and animals face the danger of extinction today. Many programs like social forestry and Van Mahotsava should be popularised at regional and community levels. This will increase awareness.
(b) How do Van Mahotsava and social forestry help restore ecological balance?
questions.solution: Van Mahotsav: trees are planted every year (first week of July), steadily increasing green cover and creating awareness. Social forestry: planting trees on community/waste land, roadsides and village commons meets local needs of fuel, fodder and timber, reducing people's dependence on natural forests, which are thereby preserved as habitats.

marking_points.point: Van Mahotsav increases green cover through annual tree planting
Social forestry reduces dependence on natural forests

questions.question:
Study the picture and answer.
(a) Name the agent responsible for the erosion seen in the picture.
questions.solution: Running water - the picture shows gully erosion (deep channels/ravines cut by water flowing over soft soil).
questions.figure_desc: Photograph of deep gullies and ravines cut into soft soil below a flat field with trees

questions.question:
Study the picture and answer.
(b) What may be done to restore the soil in such areas?
questions.solution: Plug the gullies with check dams/bunds of stones, earth or vegetation; level and terrace the land; plant trees, shrubs and grasses (afforestation) on the slopes so roots bind the soil and slow runoff.

marking_points.point: Afforestation / planting grass to bind soil

questions.question:
Answer the following:
(a) Name two major eutrophication-causing nutrients.
questions.solution: Nitrogen (nitrates) and phosphorus (phosphates).

questions.question:
Answer the following:
(b) Based on your answer, how do these nutrients cause eutrophication in water bodies?
questions.solution: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus (from fertiliser runoff and sewage) enter water bodies and cause excessive growth of algae (algal bloom). The bloom blocks sunlight from submerged plants; when the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up dissolved oxygen, so fish and other aquatic life die and the water becomes polluted.

marking_points.point: Nutrients cause excessive algal growth (algal bloom), blocking sunlight
Decay of algae depletes oxygen, killing aquatic life

questions.question:
When mixed in water, DDT accumulates in the cells of various aquatic organisms. Small fish consume zooplanktons that have DDT in them. Larger fish that consume small fish also consume DDT, and its concentration moves up the food chain.
(a) Based on the example given above, identify and name the process.
questions.solution: Biomagnification (biological magnification) - increase in concentration of a toxic substance at successive levels of a food chain.

questions.question:
When mixed in water, DDT accumulates in the cells of various aquatic organisms. Small fish consume zooplanktons that have DDT in them. Larger fish that consume small fish also consume DDT, and its concentration moves up the food chain.
(b) How do they adversely affect human health?
questions.solution: Humans at the top of the food chain eat contaminated fish and receive the highest concentration of DDT, which accumulates in body fat and can cause cancer, liver damage, nervous/respiratory disorders, heart disease, hormonal problems and birth defects.

marking_points.point: Humans at top of food chain get highest concentration
Diseases: cancer, liver failure, birth defects etc.
